title: Turnover Recognition Reset
objective: Develop players’ ability to immediately recognise whether their team has gained or lost possession and adopt the correct attacking or defensive position without waiting for further instruction.
groundSize: 30 metres long × 25 metres wide, divided into one central possession area and four outside positioning gates.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge and one main teaching point
setup:
Mark a central 20-metre × 20-metre possession area.
Place two wide attacking gates outside the left and right edges of the area.
Place two narrow defensive gates closer to the corridor.
Divide players into two evenly numbered teams.
One team begins with the football while the other team shadows without applying contact.
The coach stands outside the area with spare footballs.
howTheDrillWorks:
The team in possession moves the football by kick or handball inside the central area.
Players without possession maintain light shadow pressure but cannot intercept initially.
The coach calls “turnover” and either gives the football to the other team or rolls a new football into the area.
Players must immediately call either “ours” or “theirs” according to the new possession state.
The team gaining possession spreads towards the two wide attacking gates.
The team losing possession compresses towards the two central defensive gates.
Players hold their new structure for three seconds before play resumes.
After several repetitions, allow defenders to intercept naturally so the turnover cue becomes less predictable.
Rotate the starting team after each one-minute block.
coachingPoints: Players must identify possession change before beginning their movement.
Encourage loud, early communication from more than one player.
The team gaining possession should create width and depth rather than crowding the football.
The team losing possession should protect the corridor before chasing outside.
Players nearest the football should respond differently from players positioned further away.
Avoid all players reacting directly towards the football.
Players should scan before the turnover so their first movement is informed.
Reinforce immediate role change without disappointment, hesitation or argument.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players recognise the change of possession immediately.
Whether attacking players create usable width and depth.
Whether defensive players compress towards dangerous central space.
Whether players continue performing their previous role after possession changes.
Whether the nearest players and furthest players adopt appropriate different responses.

commonErrors.error: Players continue moving as though their team still has possession.
commonErrors.correction: Stop the repetition and require players to call “ours” or “theirs” before moving.

commonErrors.error: Every player runs directly towards the football.
commonErrors.correction: Assign outside players responsibility for width and inside players responsibility for corridor protection.

commonErrors.error: Players react only after the coach gives a second instruction.
commonErrors.correction: Remove the second instruction and reward the first team that reorganises independently.

commonErrors.error: Communication comes after the movement has already started.
commonErrors.correction: Require the possession call to be made immediately when the football changes teams.

commonErrors.error: Players walk into their transition positions.
commonErrors.correction: Set a three-second movement target while keeping the drill non-contact.

progressions: Allow defenders to intercept passes naturally rather than relying on the coach’s turnover call.
Add a three-second scoring bonus when the attacking team reaches a wide gate quickly.
Add a central scoring gate that the defending team must protect.
Increase the number of players and enlarge the area.
Allow full live play for 15-second periods after each turnover.
regressions: Use only four players per team.
Walk players through the attacking and defensive shapes before beginning.
Use a whistle and clear visual signal for each possession change.
Remove the football and practise the movements as a recognition exercise.
Give each player a fixed attacking and defensive starting position.
successIndicators: Change direction within one second of the turnover.
Protect central space before chasing wide.
Perform the transition response without waiting for the coach.
matchApplication: Australian football regularly changes from attack to defence or defence to attack without a stoppage. Players who recognise the turnover quickly can create an immediate numerical advantage, close dangerous space, provide an outlet or prevent the opposition from using the corridor.

title: Attack-to-Defence Recovery
primarySkill: Recovering defensively after losing possession in attack.
objective: Develop the ability to recover from an attacking position into an organised defensive shape immediately after possession is lost.
groundSize: 50 metres long × 35 metres wide with an attacking scoring zone, a central recovery line and a counterattack scoring gate.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Mark an attacking scoring zone at one end of the area.
Mark a counterattack gate at the opposite end.
Place a recovery line approximately 15 metres behind the attacking scoring zone.
Divide players into an attacking team and a defending team.
Begin with the attacking team positioned ahead of the recovery line.
Position the defending team compactly near the scoring zone.
The coach stands near the attacking end with spare footballs.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with possession and attempts to enter the scoring zone.
The defending team applies controlled pressure and attempts to intercept or win the football.
When the defending team gains possession, it immediately counterattacks towards the opposite scoring gate.
The player nearest the turnover applies pressure to delay the counterattack.
Other former attacking players sprint goal-side and recover through or towards the central recovery line.
Recovering players must protect the corridor before defending wider options.
The counterattacking team scores two points for reaching the opposite gate and one point for carrying or disposing through the recovery line.
The recovering team scores one point for forcing the football wide and two points for regaining possession before the opposition reaches the gate.
Reset after a score, turnover, boundary exit or 30 seconds of play.
Swap attacking and defending roles after four repetitions.
coachingPoints: The nearest player should pressure and delay rather than attempting an unrealistic immediate tackle.
Players further from the football must recover goal-side at speed.
Recovery runs should be directed towards dangerous space, not simply towards an opponent.
Protect the corridor before defending lower-risk boundary space.
Players should communicate who is pressuring, covering and protecting the deepest option.
Defenders must avoid running past the ball carrier and opening a central lane.
Once the counterattack is slowed, the defensive group should balance and match opponents.
Transition running should continue until the defence is organised, not only until players cross the recovery line.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the nearest player delays the counterattack.
The direction and speed of recovery runs.
Whether recovering players identify the most dangerous opponent.
Whether communication establishes clear defensive roles.
Whether players stop running once they reach the recovery line.
Whether the team can convert frantic recovery into an organised defensive shape.

commonErrors.error: Players chase the football from behind.
commonErrors.correction: Direct off-ball players to recover goal-side and protect the corridor.

commonErrors.error: The nearest player dives in and is evaded.
commonErrors.correction: Coach the player to close space under control and delay the disposal.

commonErrors.error: Recovering players run towards wide opponents first.
commonErrors.correction: Prioritise central space and the deepest dangerous option.

commonErrors.error: Players jog after losing possession.
commonErrors.correction: Score transition effort and rotate players who repeatedly fail to recover.

commonErrors.error: Defenders recover to the same line with no depth.
commonErrors.correction: Establish pressure, cover and deeper balance roles.

progressions: Introduce full tackling.
Add an extra counterattacking player to create numerical disadvantage.
Begin the attacking team deeper inside the scoring zone.
Allow the counterattacking team only eight seconds to score.
Require the recovering team to win possession and immediately counterattack back.
Increase the field width to create more difficult defensive decisions.
regressions: Give the recovering team a numerical advantage.
Require the counterattacking team to complete one sideways disposal before advancing.
Use touch pressure rather than tackling.
Reduce the required recovery distance for Over 35 players or returning players.
successIndicators: Protect the corridor before wide space.
Communicate dangerous opponents and open space.
Prevent direct, uncontested counterattack through the centre.
matchApplication: When a team turns the football over during an attacking phase, many players may be positioned ahead of the ball. Effective attack-to-defence transition requires immediate pressure and purposeful recovery to prevent the opposition from counterattacking through an exposed corridor.

title: Defence-to-Attack Spread
primarySkill: Spreading into attacking positions after regaining possession.
objective: Develop an immediate and coordinated attacking spread after a defensive regain so the ball carrier has safe, progressive and clearly separated disposal options.
groundSize: 40 metres long × 35 metres wide with four outlet gates positioned outside a compact defensive zone.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Mark a compact 20-metre × 20-metre defensive zone in the centre of the area.
Position two wide outlet gates on each side of the area.
Position one forward gate and one deeper safety gate.
Divide players into a defending team and an attacking pressure team.
The defending team begins compactly inside the central zone.
The pressure team begins around the outside and sends the football into the zone.
The coach stands outside the area with spare footballs.
howTheDrillWorks:
The pressure team kicks or handballs the football into the central defensive zone.
The defending team attempts to intercept, mark, spoil to advantage or win the ground ball.
Once possession is secured, the defending team immediately becomes the attacking team.
The first player outside the contest provides width on the nearest side.
A second player creates an option on the opposite side.
One player pushes forward while another remains behind the football as a safety option.
The team must exit through one of the four outlet gates while retaining possession.
Two points are awarded for using a forward or opposite-side outlet and one point for using the nearest safe outlet.
The opposition applies controlled pressure and attempts to lock the football inside the central zone.
Reset when the football exits through a gate, is turned over or leaves the playing area.
coachingPoints: The first attacking movement should create separation from the contest.
Players should spread to different lanes rather than following the same path.
The player winning possession must be supported from the front, side and behind.
Width should be created before the opposition can establish a press.
The ball carrier should use the safest progressive option, not automatically the nearest teammate.
Opposite-side players must remain engaged and available for a switch.
Players should avoid all running forward and leaving no support behind the football.
Communication should identify wide, forward and safety options.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: How quickly players leave the compact defensive shape.
Whether players create width on both sides.
Whether forward and safety options are available.
Whether players crowd the first possession.
Whether the ball carrier scans the full field.
Whether the team selects a safe but progressive exit.
Whether the opposite side remains available for a switch.

commonErrors.error: Players remain in a defensive cluster after winning possession.
commonErrors.correction: Use outlet gates to give each player a clear spreading responsibility.

commonErrors.error: All players run forward.
commonErrors.correction: Require one designated safety player to remain behind the football.

commonErrors.error: Players spread to the same side.
commonErrors.correction: Allocate near-side, far-side, forward and rear support roles.

commonErrors.error: The ball carrier uses the closest option without scanning.
commonErrors.correction: Require a visible head turn before disposal.

commonErrors.error: Wide players move too early and become disconnected.
commonErrors.correction: Time the spread to occur as possession is being secured.

progressions: Allow full pressure after possession is won.
Add a second disposal requirement before the team can exit.
Award extra points for switching to the opposite side.
Reduce the width of the outlet gates.
Add a recovering defender outside the central zone.
Continue play into a second attacking phase after the exit.
regressions: Remove opposition pressure after the regain.
Nominate the required exit before the repetition.
Allow the coach to pause play and reposition players.
Use handball only for younger players.
successIndicators: Spread within two seconds of the regain.
Create width on both sides of the contest.
Exit without crowding the ball carrier.
Retain possession through the first exit.
matchApplication: After an intercept mark, spoil recovery or ground-ball win in defence, players must quickly expand from a compact defensive shape into an attacking shape. Effective spread creates exit options before the opposition can establish repeat pressure.

title: Boundary Contest Rebound
primarySkill: Rebounding from a contested possession near the boundary.
objective: Develop the ability to secure a boundary-side contest and transition into open space without forcing a high-risk central disposal.
groundSize: 40 metres long × 30 metres wide with a narrow boundary contest lane and two exit gates.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a five-metre-wide contest lane along one boundary.
Place a safe boundary exit gate ahead of the contest.
Place a higher-value central release gate on the opposite side of the area.
Divide players into two teams.
Position three to five players from each team near the contest lane.
Position outside support players through the central and far-side space.
The coach begins each repetition with a ground ball, high ball or pressured pass into the boundary lane.
howTheDrillWorks:
Both teams contest for the football inside the boundary lane.
The team gaining possession must establish control before selecting an exit.
A nearby teammate provides a safe down-the-line option.
Central and far-side players provide release options away from the boundary.
The boundary gate scores one point.
The central release gate scores three points but may only be used when the receiver has clear separation.
A central turnover gives the opposition three points.
The team losing possession applies immediate pressure and attempts to trap the football near the boundary.
Play continues until an exit, turnover, stoppage or 30-second limit.
Alternate the starting boundary after four repetitions.
coachingPoints: Secure possession before attempting to move away from the boundary.
The safe down-the-line option should remain available.
Central release should be used only when the lane is genuinely clear.
Support players must not all enter the boundary congestion.
The ball winner should protect the football from boundary-side pressure.
Players behind the football should provide a reset.
The defending team should use the boundary as an extra defender.
Far-side players must remain engaged as potential switch options.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the ball winner protects possession.
Whether safe and aggressive exits are both available.
Whether defenders trap the football against the boundary.
Whether the team can later access central space after securing possession.

commonErrors.error: Players attempt an immediate blind disposal into the corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Secure the football and confirm the central receiver is clear.

commonErrors.error: All teammates crowd the boundary contest.
commonErrors.correction: Keep outside players in release positions.

commonErrors.error: The ball carrier steps over the boundary unnecessarily.
commonErrors.correction: Protect the football while maintaining awareness of the line.

commonErrors.error: Players ignore the safe down-the-line option.
commonErrors.correction: Retain a boundary outlet when the centre is closed.

commonErrors.error: Defenders allow an easy inside release.
commonErrors.correction: Pressure from the corridor side and force play towards the line.

progressions: Reduce the contest-lane width.
Add full controlled tackling.
Remove the marked exit gates.
Require a switch after a successful boundary exit.
Add a recovering defender in central space.
Continue into a full-ground transition phase.
regressions: Give the ball-winning team an extra outside player.
Stop briefly after possession is secured.
Reduce contact for younger or returning players.
successIndicators: Secure contested possession near the boundary.
Use central space only when clearly available.
Escape the boundary pressure with retained possession.
matchApplication: Boundary contests reduce space and often attract numbers. Teams must secure the football, maintain a safe outlet and recognise when central space is genuinely available rather than forcing a dangerous release.

title: Corridor Break and Hold Width
primarySkill: Breaking through the corridor while preserving outside width.
objective: Develop a central transition that attacks through the corridor without drawing every supporting player into the same lane.
groundSize: 75 metres long × 55 metres wide with a central corridor and two outside support lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a central corridor approximately 15 metres wide.
Mark one outside support lane on each side.
Place a scoring gate at the attacking end.
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Begin the transitioning team with possession near the defensive end.
Position defenders to pressure the corridor progressively.
Require at least one attacking player to remain in each outside lane.
howTheDrillWorks:
The transitioning team attempts to move possession through the corridor.
Central receivers lead into space and release before pressure closes.
Outside players hold width and remain available for release.
If the corridor remains open, the team may continue directly.
If defenders collapse centrally, the football is released to an outside lane.
One point is awarded for each controlled corridor possession.
Two points are awarded for breaking beyond the midfield line.
A bonus point is awarded when both outside lanes remain occupied.
Two additional points are awarded for reaching the scoring gate.
Defenders receive three points for forcing a central turnover.
Roles reverse immediately after a turnover.
Reset after a score, turnover or 40 seconds.
coachingPoints: Corridor players should receive while moving.
Outside players must resist following the football centrally.
The ball carrier should scan wide before central pressure arrives.
Width provides an escape and stretches the defence.
Support should remain behind as well as ahead of possession.
Central disposals must lead receivers away from pressure.
The team should avoid forcing corridor play when numbers close.
Players must transition defensively after a central turnover.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether central receivers scan before possession.
Quality of disposals through the corridor.
Whether safety support remains behind the football.
Defensive reaction after a central turnover.

commonErrors.error: Every player follows the football into the corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain one option in each outside lane.

commonErrors.error: Central receivers stand still.
commonErrors.correction: Lead into the corridor as the previous player prepares to dispose.

commonErrors.error: The team forces the next central possession.
commonErrors.correction: Release wide when the corridor compresses.

commonErrors.error: Wide players become too disconnected.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust width so they remain within achievable disposal distance.

commonErrors.error: No player protects behind the central chain.
commonErrors.correction: Retain a trailing security player.

progressions: Remove the lane markers.
Add full match-like pressure.
Reduce the corridor width.
Add a recovering defender from behind.
Continue into a live forward entry.
Introduce scoreboard conditions that alter risk.
regressions: Reduce repeat running for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Release to outside space when required.
Prevent central turnovers from becoming direct scores.
matchApplication: Corridor transition can move the football quickly towards goal, but it becomes dangerous when every player compresses centrally. Maintaining outside width protects possession and preserves alternative routes.

title: False Corridor Entry
primarySkill: Using apparent corridor movement to create outside transition space.
objective: Develop coordinated movement that presents a credible corridor threat before releasing possession into outside space created by defensive compression.
groundSize: 75 metres long × 55 metres wide with a central corridor and two wide scoring lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a central corridor approximately 15 metres wide.
Mark a wide scoring lane on each side.
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Position two central attacking receivers and wide players on both sides.
Begin with a defensive or midfield regain.
Position defenders to react strongly to central leads.
Retain at least one safety player behind the football.
howTheDrillWorks:
The transitioning team secures possession.
One or two central players lead visibly into the corridor.
The ball carrier presents as though the next disposal will travel centrally.
Defenders compress towards the corridor leads.
Wide players hold their lanes and prepare to receive.
The ball carrier releases to the side offering the greatest space.
One point is awarded when central movement draws defenders.
Two points are awarded for completing the wide release.
Two additional points are awarded for reaching a wide scoring gate.
Defenders receive three points for holding width and intercepting the release.
Roles reverse after a turnover.
Reset after a score, turnover or 40 seconds.
coachingPoints: The corridor movement must be credible enough to influence defenders.
Central players should not obstruct each other or become stationary targets.
Wide players must maintain width and timing.
The ball carrier should scan both sides before presenting centrally.
Release timing is critical once defenders compress.
Safety support must remain behind the initial movement.
The corridor may still be used when defenders fail to compress.
Players must avoid turning the pattern into a predetermined fake.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the central leads appear genuine.
Timing and direction of the release.
Whether the ball carrier scans both sides.
Whether the team uses the corridor when it remains available.
Whether defensive balance remains behind the football.

commonErrors.error: Central players make token movements that do not influence defenders.
commonErrors.correction: Lead with speed and present as genuine receiving options.

commonErrors.error: Wide players drift in before the release.
commonErrors.correction: Hold width until the defence commits centrally.

commonErrors.error: The ball carrier decides the release side before scanning.
commonErrors.correction: Assess both wide lanes after defenders move.

commonErrors.error: The team refuses an open corridor because the drill expects width.
commonErrors.correction: Use the central option when defenders do not close it.

commonErrors.error: Security players follow the central leads.
commonErrors.correction: Remain connected behind possession.

progressions: Remove the corridor and lane markers.
Add full match-like pressure.
Allow defenders to disguise whether they will compress.
Introduce a second wide release after the first is closed.
Continue into a forward-entry phase.
Add scoreboard and time pressure.
regressions: Give the transitioning team a numerical advantage.
Reduce the number of central receivers.
successIndicators: Retain the corridor when it remains open.
matchApplication: Teams can create outside transition space by presenting a genuine central threat. Defenders who compress towards the corridor may leave wide lanes available for fast release.
relatedDrills: TR-072 – Corridor Break and Hold Width

title: Floating Player Transition Rotation
primarySkill: Integrating a floating player without losing team balance.
objective: Develop coordinated use of a floating transition player while ensuring teammates rotate to maintain width, line connection and defensive security.
groundSize: 75 metres long × 50 metres wide with defensive, midfield and attacking thirds.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the field into defensive, midfield and attacking thirds.
Divide players into two teams.
Add one neutral floating player who supports the team in possession.
The floating player may move anywhere.
Begin each phase with a defensive or midfield regain.
Require teams to maintain at least two players behind the football.
Rotate the floating role every three minutes.
howTheDrillWorks:
One team gains possession and may use the floating player.
The floating player moves to become the most useful transition connection.
A teammate must rotate to preserve team width or security when the float moves.
The team receives one point for using the float to complete a line-breaking possession.
One point is awarded for a successful role rotation around the float.
Two points are awarded for entering the attacking third.
Two additional points are awarded for scoring.
If the football turns over, the float immediately supports the new attacking team.
Both teams must reorganise around the float’s new position.
A turnover caused by losing behind-ball security gives the opposition a bonus point.
Play in three-minute blocks.
Rotate the float and restart from varied locations.
coachingPoints: The floating player should move to solve the current transition problem.
Teammates must not simply follow the float.
When the float moves forward, another player may need to replace behind.
When the float moves wide, central connection must remain.
The float should communicate the role being provided.
Players must reorganise immediately after a turnover.
The team should avoid overusing the neutral player when direct options exist.
The float must receive in space with a clear next action.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the float moves to a useful location.
Whether teammates rotate around the movement.
Whether width and security are preserved.
Whether the team overuses the floating player.
Whether the float has a next option.
Whether the float communicates the role being provided.

commonErrors.error: Teammates crowd around the floating player.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain normal spacing and use the float as one option.

commonErrors.error: The float runs ahead and leaves no security.
commonErrors.correction: Require a teammate to replace behind before the movement continues.

commonErrors.error: Players automatically dispose to the neutral player.
commonErrors.correction: Use direct team options when they provide greater advantage.

commonErrors.error: The float receives without a next action.
commonErrors.correction: Move into positions that connect at least two teammates or lines.

commonErrors.error: Teams react slowly when the float changes sides after turnover.
commonErrors.correction: Reorganise immediately around the new possession team.

progressions: Add a second floating player with different movement restrictions.
Limit the number of float possessions.
Add full match-like pressure.
Remove the marked thirds.
Introduce scoreboard and time conditions.
Allow the defending team to temporarily deny the float.
regressions: Restrict the float to the midfield third.
Stop after turnovers to review rotations.
Keep three players behind the football.
Use shorter blocks for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Use the float to connect lines or break pressure.
matchApplication: Some players naturally become transition connectors by moving across positional lines. The team must use their movement without abandoning width, role balance or protection behind the football.

title: Midfield Unit Transition Roles
objective: Develop coordinated transition roles for inside midfielders, outside midfielders and defensive midfield support during repeated possession changes.
groundSize: Central 80 metres of the ground, including the centre square and both half-back and half-forward areas.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a central playing area extending from half-back to half-forward.
Place a scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two midfield units.
Within each unit, identify:
Inside ball winner
Defensive midfielder
Forward-running midfielder
Outside midfielder
Underneath support midfielder
Begin from stoppages, loose footballs and coach-created turnovers.
Rotate roles every four repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
Play begins with a midfield contest or controlled possession.
When a team gains possession, the inside ball winner secures and releases the football.
The outside midfielder provides width.
The forward-running midfielder moves ahead into attacking connection.
The underneath midfielder supports behind the football.
When possession is lost, the nearest midfielder pressures.
The defensive midfielder protects the corridor and tracks the most dangerous runner.
Other midfielders recover goal-side and reconnect with defenders.
The attacking team receives one point for exiting the contest and two points for reaching its scoring gate.
The defending team receives one point for forcing a backwards disposal and three for regaining possession.
Play continues through repeated turnovers for up to 45 seconds.
Reset and review role execution after each repetition.
coachingPoints: Inside midfielders must secure possession before releasing.
Outside midfielders should preserve width rather than entering every contest.
One midfielder should support underneath the football.
Forward runners must time movement to possession security.
The nearest player pressures after a turnover.
Defensive midfielders protect the corridor and dangerous runners.
Midfielders must work in both directions rather than specialising in one phase.
Communication should identify inside, outside, hold, recover and deepest roles.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether role clarity remains under fatigue.

commonErrors.error: Every midfielder attacks the initial contest.
commonErrors.correction: Hold one outside player and one underneath support player.

commonErrors.error: Forward runners leave before possession is secure.
commonErrors.correction: Time the run to the ball winner’s control.

commonErrors.error: No midfielder supports behind the football.
commonErrors.correction: Assign an underneath connection and security role.

commonErrors.error: Midfielders chase direct opponents into wide space.
commonErrors.correction: Protect the corridor and most dangerous runner first.

commonErrors.error: Players perform only attacking or defensive work.
commonErrors.correction: Rotate roles and score two-way transition actions.

progressions: Remove marked midfield roles.
Add full match-like stoppage contact.
Introduce changing numerical balance.
Continue from midfield into full forward entries.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Require role handovers during the same phase.
regressions: Give the possession team a neutral midfielder.
Shorten repeated running for Over 35 players.
matchApplication: Midfielders are central to transition because they influence both the initial contest and the connection between defence and attack. Effective midfield units maintain role balance rather than sending every player towards the same action.

title: Wing Transition Roles
primarySkill: Executing wing-specific attacking and defensive transition roles.
objective: Develop wing players’ ability to provide attacking width, switch connection and defensive corridor support according to ball location and possession state.
groundSize: Approximately 80 metres long × 60 metres wide, using both wings and the corridor.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a near-side wing, corridor and far-side wing.
Place one scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two teams.
Assign one wing player to each side for both teams.
Position other players through half-back, midfield and half-forward.
Begin from defensive and midfield regains on alternating sides.
Rotate wing players every four repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
One team gains possession near a boundary or through the corridor.
The near-side wing provides an immediate outside or forward option.
The far-side wing holds width and prepares for a switch.
If the team loses possession, the near-side wing pressures or tracks the outside outlet.
The far-side wing folds towards the corridor while preserving far-side awareness.
When possession changes again, both wings expand quickly.
One point is awarded for effective near-side support.
One point is awarded for maintaining usable far-side width.
Two points are awarded for a successful switch through a wing.
The defending team receives two points when a wing’s recovery closes a dangerous lane.
Play continues through repeated turnovers for 40 seconds.
Reset and alternate the starting side.
coachingPoints: Near-side and far-side wing roles differ.
The near-side wing should support the immediate possession phase.
The far-side wing must maintain width without becoming disconnected.
After losing possession, wings should fold enough to protect the corridor.
Wings must scan inside and behind, not only follow the boundary.
Far-side width can become the best attacking option after a regain.
Wing players should preserve the ability to move in both directions.
Communication should identify switch, fold, hold and inside support.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Position of near-side and far-side wings.
Whether wings fold appropriately in defence.
Whether wing receivers have inside support.
Whether players become trapped against the boundary.

commonErrors.error: Both wings move to the same side of the ground.
commonErrors.correction: Preserve far-side width and team balance.

commonErrors.error: The far-side wing remains too wide after possession is lost.
commonErrors.correction: Fold towards the corridor while tracking the switch threat.

commonErrors.error: The near-side wing stands flat-footed.
commonErrors.correction: Lead into space and provide a moving outlet.

commonErrors.error: Wings receive without inside support.
commonErrors.correction: Connect a midfielder or half-back beneath the wing.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after a switch disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Continue supporting the next forward action.

progressions: Remove wing-lane markers.
Add full match-like pressure.
Require wing players to rotate with half-backs and half-forwards.
Continue into a full forward-entry phase.
Introduce hidden switch traps.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
regressions: Stop after each turnover to review wing positioning.
Reduce repeated running for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Execute different near-side and far-side roles.
matchApplication: Wing players provide critical balance during transition. Their positioning determines whether the team can access width in attack while still protecting the corridor and opposite-side movement in defence.
relatedDrills: TR-063 – Wing Release and Inside Support

title: Forward Unit Transition Roles
primarySkill: Executing forward-specific transition roles after gaining or losing possession.
objective: Develop clear transition roles for deep forwards, high forwards and pressure forwards during forward entries, defensive exits and forward-half regains.
groundSize: Forward half of an oval, including forward 50 and high half-forward space.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use one forward half.
Divide players into a forward unit and defensive unit.
Within the forward unit, identify:
Deep forward
High forward
Pressure forwards
Forward-half security player
Mark near-side, corridor and far-side defensive exits.
Begin each repetition with a forward entry.
Vary whether the entry is marked, spoiled, intercepted or won at ground level.
howTheDrillWorks:
The forward unit organises leads and support during the entry.
If the forward team wins possession, it attempts to create a controlled scoring opportunity.
If the defensive team regains possession, forward roles immediately change.
The nearest pressure forward closes the ball carrier.
Other pressure forwards deny the short and corridor exits.
The high forward protects the next release or midfield connection.
The deep forward either pressures locally or protects the dangerous switch route according to position.
If the forward team regains possession, players spread into direct, wide and underneath scoring options.
The forward unit receives three points for a goal and two points for a repeat entry.
The defensive unit receives three points for a controlled exit.
Play continues for up to 40 seconds.
Reset and rotate forward roles.
coachingPoints: Forward transition begins immediately when an entry is lost.
The nearest forward pressures while others close exits.
High forwards must protect the connection beyond defensive 50.
Deep forwards should avoid chasing harmless possession away from goal.
Forward-half regains should be secured before a rushed shot.
Players must create varied scoring options after regaining possession.
At least one player should remain behind the attacking contest.
Communication should identify pressure, corridor, switch and deepest roles.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Reaction after a lost forward entry.
Coverage of corridor and short exits.

commonErrors.error: Every forward chases the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Assign pressure, outlet-denial and deeper-cover roles.

commonErrors.error: The high forward moves too deep into the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Hold position to protect the next defensive exit.

commonErrors.error: Deep forwards stop after an intercepted entry.
commonErrors.correction: Pressure locally or protect the dangerous route.

commonErrors.error: Forward-half regains produce rushed shots.
commonErrors.correction: Secure possession and improve the scoring opportunity.

commonErrors.error: No player remains behind the attacking contest.
commonErrors.correction: Retain forward-half security against another turnover.

progressions: Add full match-like defensive pressure.
Remove the marked defensive exits.
Introduce different defensive exit systems.
Continue play to the opposite end after a successful exit.
Add scoreboard and late-game scenarios.
Allow forward players to rotate roles during the same phase.
regressions: Give the forward unit a numerical advantage.
Begin with a controlled forward-half regain.
Reduce repeat efforts for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: React immediately after losing an entry.
Apply pressure through the nearest forward.
matchApplication: Forwards influence transition both by creating scoring options and by preventing defensive exits. Clear forward roles help generate repeat entries without exposing the team to easy counterattack.

title: Ruck and Stoppage Transition Roles
primarySkill: Executing ruck and stoppage-specific transition responsibilities.
objective: Develop coordinated transition roles for rucks, inside midfielders and outside stoppage players immediately after the stoppage outcome becomes clear.
groundSize: A 25-metre stoppage area inside a 65-metre × 45-metre transition field.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a central stoppage circle or throw-in area.
Place a scoring gate at each end.
Divide players into two stoppage units.
Within each unit, identify:
Ruck
First-possession midfielder
Defensive midfielder
Outside midfielder
High support player
Begin from ball-ups, boundary throw-ins and ground-ball stoppage simulations.
Rotate roles across several starts.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins the stoppage.
The rucks compete and follow the football after the hit-out.
Inside midfielders attempt to secure the first possession.
Outside players hold shape until the football’s direction becomes clear.
The team winning possession releases outside or forward.
The team losing possession pressures the clearance source.
The defensive midfielder protects the corridor and tracks the first forward runner.
The ruck either supports the clearance or folds behind the football.
One point is awarded for winning the first possession.
Two points are awarded for exiting the stoppage area under control.
Two additional points are awarded for reaching a scoring gate.
Reset after a score, turnover, secondary stoppage or 35 seconds.
coachingPoints: Rucks must transition after the hit-out rather than watching the outcome.
Inside midfielders should secure possession before forcing clearance.
Outside players must hold width and avoid collapsing early.
The team losing possession should pressure the source immediately.
Defensive midfielders protect the corridor and dangerous runners.
The ruck can become a support or defensive security player.
Players must react to the actual hit-out rather than the planned one.
Communication should identify possession, pressure, outside and recovery roles.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Ruck support behind or beside the football.

commonErrors.error: The ruck stops after the tap.
commonErrors.correction: Follow the football and become support or pressure.

commonErrors.error: Outside midfielders collapse into the stoppage.
commonErrors.correction: Hold width until possession direction is clear.

commonErrors.error: The clearance player kicks blindly.
commonErrors.correction: Secure possession and use an outside or supported release.

commonErrors.error: Defensive midfielders chase the football.
commonErrors.correction: Protect the corridor and dangerous forward runner.

commonErrors.error: Players move according to the planned hit rather than the actual outcome.
commonErrors.correction: Read the live football and adjust immediately.

progressions: Add full match-like stoppage contact.
Remove fixed stoppage roles.
Introduce numerical imbalance outside the contest.
Continue into full-ground play.
Add scoreboard and late-game stoppage scenarios.
Run consecutive stoppages without positional reset.
regressions: Give one team an extra outside player.
Reduce repeat efforts for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Follow the hit-out with a second action.
Use the ruck as support or security.
Transition from stoppage into open play.
matchApplication: Stoppages create immediate transition moments once possession becomes clear. Rucks and midfielders must move from set stoppage roles into open-play attack or defence without hesitation.

title: Match Scenario Transition Simulation
primarySkill: Applying complete transition systems across realistic match scenarios.
objective: Prepare players for the final chapter assessment by integrating position-specific roles, turnover-zone responses, match context and full-ground transition under realistic pressure.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use the full oval.
Divide players into two balanced match teams.
Establish normal positional structures.
Prepare six scenarios:
Defensive 50 regain against a high press
Midfield turnover with numerical advantage
Midfield turnover while outnumbered
Forward-half regain
Kick-in transition
Red-time scoreboard transition
Assign coaching observers to defence, midfield, wings and forwards.
Player leaders manage communication and structure.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins Scenario 1 and allows play to continue until the objective is completed or possession stabilises.
The next scenario starts immediately from a different field position.
Players must reorganise without a complete positional reset.
Position groups execute their transition responsibilities.
Normal match scoring applies.
One team-structure point is awarded for maintaining line connection.
One decision-quality point is awarded for selecting an appropriate transition response.
One defensive point is awarded for organised pressure and recovery after losing possession.
An avoidable turnover caused by poor transition balance removes one point.
Complete the six-scenario sequence twice.
On the second sequence, alter opposition tactics and scoreboard conditions.
Finish with five minutes of unrestricted play.
coachingPoints: Position-specific roles must support the whole-team response.
Players should recognise field position before selecting transition speed.
Numerical advantage should be used before it disappears.
Numerical disadvantage should be managed through security and delay.
Defensive 50 regains require calm exit connection.
Forward-half regains require organised scoring and pressure.
Kick-in structure must flow into open play.
Red-time scenarios alter risk and tempo.
Leadership communication should organise without removing player decision making.
Transition behaviours must remain during unrestricted play.

commonErrors.error: Position groups perform their roles without connecting to teammates.
commonErrors.correction: Judge every role by its effect on the complete team structure.

commonErrors.error: Players wait for a full reset between scenarios.
commonErrors.correction: Reorganise immediately from the current field position.

commonErrors.error: The same transition route is used repeatedly.
commonErrors.correction: Read pressure, field position and available numbers.

commonErrors.error: Leaders give constant instructions that slow decisions.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate essential information and allow teammates to act.

commonErrors.error: Structure disappears during unrestricted play.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce the same principles without drill scoring or coach prompts.

progressions: Allow opposition teams to create their own scenarios.
Remove all coach announcements.
Increase match-like contact.
Add quarter-length scoreboard simulation.
Use video and GPS data where available.
Include special situations such as a player off the ground or deliberate defensive spare.
regressions: Shorten the simulation for Over 35 players.
matchApplication: This simulation combines the position-specific, tactical and contextual demands of transition. It tests whether the team can move between different match situations without relying on complete resets or constant coach direction.

title: Transition Chapter Final Assessment
primarySkill: Demonstrating complete individual, positional and team transition capability.
objective: Complete the final assessment of the Transition chapter by evaluating whether players and the team can independently recognise, organise and execute all major transition behaviours under full match conditions.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use the full oval.
Divide players into two balanced match teams.
Use normal positional structures and rotations.
Assign observers to assess:
Individual transition reaction
Defensive unit
Midfield unit
Wings
Forward unit
Whole-team shape
Match-context decision making
Prepare assessment categories covering the full chapter:
Turnover recognition
First-three-second response
Immediate pressure
Corridor recovery
First-possession security
Attacking spread
Support running
Defensive exit
Team line connection
Position-specific roles
Numerical decision making
Scoreboard management
Turnover protection
Communication and leadership
Begin with normal match conditions rather than a predetermined pattern.
howTheDrillWorks:
Play begins as a full match simulation.
Coaches allow natural turnovers to occur without immediate intervention.
During the first block, no bonus points or coach prompts are used.
During the second block, the coach introduces selected scenarios including:
Defensive 50 regain
Central turnover
Forward-half regain
Stoppage spill
Kick-in
Numerical imbalance
Red-time scoreboard situation
Normal match scoring applies throughout.
Individual players are assessed on recognition, effort, role execution and decision quality.
Position groups are assessed on connection and role clarity.
The whole team is assessed on shape change, route selection and turnover protection.
Play four blocks of eight to ten minutes.
Give only brief principle-based feedback between blocks.
Complete the final block without coach-created scenarios or transition scoring.
Conduct a post-session review using observations, player feedback and video where available.
coachingPoints: Players must recognise turnovers independently.
The first three seconds should contain purposeful attacking or defensive action.
Nearest-player pressure must be supported by cover and balance.
Defensive recovery should protect corridor, goal-side and deepest space.
Regains must be secured through the first and second possessions.
The attacking team should create width, depth and connected support.
Defensive exits require composure and several linked actions.
Team lines must move together through full-ground transition.
Position-specific responsibilities must contribute to the complete team shape.
Numerical advantage and disadvantage must be recognised quickly.
Scoreboard, time and field position should influence risk.
High-risk transition requires protection behind the football.
Communication must be early, specific and useful.
Transition behaviours should remain without external scoring or coach prompts.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Security of the first two possessions.
Connection between defenders, midfielders, wings and forwards.

commonErrors.error: Players recognise turnovers only after teammates react.
commonErrors.correction: Scan continuously and take independent responsibility for the first action.

commonErrors.error: Pressure is applied without support behind it.
commonErrors.correction: Establish cover, corridor protection and deeper balance.

commonErrors.error: The team wins possession but loses the next disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Secure the first and second possessions before expanding fully.

commonErrors.error: Position groups become disconnected.
commonErrors.correction: Move the entire team shape with the football.

commonErrors.error: Players use the same transition response in every location.
commonErrors.correction: Match the action to field position, pressure, numbers and scoreboard.

commonErrors.error: Aggressive transition leaves no protection behind.
commonErrors.correction: Organise security before attempting high-risk movement.

commonErrors.error: Communication disappears under fatigue.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain clear role and pressure calls throughout the session.

commonErrors.error: Behaviours appear only during coach-created scenarios.
commonErrors.correction: Assess and reinforce transition habits during unrestricted play.

progressions: Extend into full quarter-length match simulation.
Use full senior match contact where appropriate.
Allow teams to design and alter their own transition systems.
Include opposition tactical changes between quarters.
Add player-number scenarios such as rotations, injuries or temporary imbalance.
Use detailed video coding and statistical transition review.
Establish individual and positional development plans from assessment results.
regressions: Assess one half of the ground at a time.
Reduce player numbers and field dimensions.
Evaluate selected transition categories rather than the full chapter.
Pause after major turnovers to review shape.
Shorten blocks and running distances for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Apply organised pressure and defensive recovery.
Secure the first and second possessions.
Create attacking width, depth and support.
Sustain repeat effort and decision quality.
Reproduce transition behaviours during unrestricted match play.
matchApplication: This final assessment represents the complete Transition chapter. It determines whether players can independently move from attack to defence and defence to attack across contests, field positions, positional roles, tactical systems and match scenarios. Successful performance indicates that transition principles have become repeatable team behaviours rather than isolated drill actions.
relatedDrills: TR-060 – Pressure and Contest Transition Assessment
TR-070 – Team Ball Movement Transition Assessment
